1. Data engineering foundations
DOMAIN 1 · TASKS 1.1, 1.2, 1.4

Volume, velocity & variety

  • Volume sets storage and scan requirements
  • Velocity determines arrival rate and freshness
  • Variety determines parsing and schema handling
  • Measure peak and sustained loads separately
Choose / applyExam distinction
Size the entire path: producer, network, transformation and sink.A fast ingestion service cannot compensate for a slow destination.
Example & explanation
  • A daily 200 GB export is a different workload from 200 GB arriving in a one-minute burst.
  • The same total volume can require different buffering, parallelism and latency budgets. Requirements drive the pipeline, rather than a favorite service.

Batch, micro-batch & streaming

  • Batch handles bounded datasets
  • Streaming handles an unbounded event sequence
  • Micro-batch groups a stream into short processing intervals
  • Freshness is measured at the consumer, not just ingestion
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use scheduled batch for daily reports and streaming for continuously updated decisions.Near-real-time delivery does not imply a fixed millisecond latency guarantee.
Example & explanation
  • A monthly billing reconciliation can use batch even when its source application is real time.
  • Batch boundaries simplify reconciliation. Streaming requires checkpoints, late-event policies and a continuously operating consumer.

ETL vs ELT & lake layers

  • ETL transforms before the analytical destination
  • ELT loads before using destination compute to transform
  • Raw preserves source fidelity
  • Curated standardizes data; serving optimizes consumption
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose Glue or EMR for distributed preprocessing; use Redshift SQL when warehouse compute should perform transformations.A raw zone is not automatically a trusted dataset.
Example & explanation
  • Raw JSON → validated Parquet → a daily sales aggregate.
  • Layer boundaries isolate replay, validation and presentation. Retaining raw inputs lets you correct transformation logic without asking every producer to resend data.

Data contracts & schema drift

  • Define required columns and types
  • Specify keys, units, nullability and timestamp timezone
  • Version incompatible changes
  • Validate producer and consumer expectations
Choose / applyExam distinction
Introduce explicit contracts when independently deployed teams share datasets.A crawler discovers structure; it does not enforce business correctness.
Example & explanation
  • Changing amount from integer cents to decimal currency is a semantic change even when parsing succeeds.
  • A structurally valid file can still produce incorrect financial results. Contracts address meaning as well as serialization.

Event time, processing time & watermarks

  • Event time describes when an event occurred
  • Processing time describes when a system handled it
  • Watermarks help bound late-data state
  • Late events need a correction or rejection policy
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use event-time windows when the result should reflect the business event timeline.A watermark is not proof that every earlier event has arrived.
Example & explanation
  • A mobile device sends yesterday's transaction after reconnecting today.
  • Out-of-order arrival is normal in distributed systems. Retention and state limits trade perfect historical completeness against bounded compute and latency.

Idempotency & delivery semantics

  • At-most-once can lose work
  • At-least-once can repeat work
  • Idempotent writes tolerate retries
  • Use stable event IDs and atomic sink operations
Choose / applyExam distinction
Combine durable checkpoints with a deduplicating destination or transactional write pattern.A checkpoint alone does not make external side effects exactly once.
Example & explanation
  • Insert an order only if its event_id has not already been committed.
  • A failure after the sink write but before checkpointing replays the record. The destination must recognize the repeated business event.

Partitioning & distributed computing

  • Partitions divide work across workers
  • Shuffles move data between partitions
  • Skew creates straggling tasks
  • A hot key can overload one partition despite idle capacity elsewhere
Choose / applyExam distinction
Partition on query or processing access patterns and observe the resulting distribution.More workers do not automatically fix a single dominant key.
Example & explanation
  • A retailer with one extremely popular product needs skew-aware joins or repartitioning.
  • Parallelism is effective only when work is sufficiently balanced and the expensive stages can run independently.

Recovery, replay & reproducibility

  • RPO measures tolerable data loss
  • RTO measures tolerable restoration time
  • Replay requires retained inputs and compatible code
  • Record input versions, job parameters and transformation version
Choose / applyExam distinction
Design recovery before the first production load.A successful job status does not prove the intended dataset is complete.
Example & explanation
  • Rebuild a failed day's curated partition from immutable raw files and the recorded code commit.
  • Reproducible pipelines make investigation and recovery repeatable. Replaying into a non-idempotent target can still duplicate valid data.

Exercise: Validate a contract and detect duplicate business events

  • Accept only orders with a nonempty event ID and a nonnegative numeric amount. Count valid, invalid and repeated events separately.
Setup
  • Python 3; no AWS account required.
Complete worked answer
  • Use the four embedded records as the input fixture.
  • Validate required fields before recording an ID as accepted.
  • Use Decimal for monetary parsing and a set for accepted event IDs.
  • Run the code twice with a fresh fixture and compare the same deterministic result.
python
from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation

rows = [
    {"event_id": "e1", "amount": "10.50"},
    {"event_id": "e1", "amount": "10.50"},
    {"event_id": "", "amount": "4.00"},
    {"event_id": "e2", "amount": "-2.00"},
]
seen, valid, invalid, duplicate = set(), [], [], []
for row in rows:
    try:
        amount = Decimal(row["amount"])
        if not row["event_id"] or not amount.is_finite() or amount < 0:
            raise ValueError("Invalid order")
    except (KeyError, InvalidOperation, ValueError):
        invalid.append(row)
        continue
    if row["event_id"] in seen:
        duplicate.append(row)
        continue
    seen.add(row["event_id"])
    valid.append(row)
print({"input": len(rows), "valid": len(valid),
       "invalid": len(invalid), "duplicate": len(duplicate)})
assert len(rows) == len(valid) + len(invalid) + len(duplicate)

Expected result

  • input = 4; valid = 1; invalid = 2; duplicate = 1.
  • The count assertion passes.

Why this works

  • Validation checks business meaning as well as type.
  • The in-memory set demonstrates one-run deduplication; production needs durable/atomic destination state across failures.

Troubleshooting

  • Do not accept NaN or Infinity as valid currency.
  • A process restart clears this set; do not mistake the demonstration for a durable exactly-once system.

Cleanup

  • No cloud resources are created.
CHAPTER 1 · Q1

A pipeline receives a complete export each night. Reports are required by 08:00, with no daytime updates. Which initial design best matches the requirement?

  1. A vector database for all source rows
  2. Scheduled batch processing with completeness validation
  3. A continuously running Flink application
  4. A separate Lambda invocation for every report query
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: B
OptionExplanation
A · A vector database for all source rowsSemantic similarity does not address the specified ingestion and reporting need.
B · Scheduled batch processing with completeness validationA bounded nightly dataset and a morning deadline fit batch processing; validate the expected batch before publication.
C · A continuously running Flink applicationContinuous stateful processing adds operational work without a stated continuous-freshness requirement.
D · A separate Lambda invocation for every report queryRepeated transformation at query time does not establish a validated nightly dataset.
CHAPTER 1 · Q2

A producer changes amount from cents to currency units without changing the column type. Every file still parses. What best prevents silent reporting errors?

  1. A versioned data contract that specifies units and validates semantic expectations
  2. Enable object versioning alone
  3. Run the crawler more frequently
  4. Increase Spark workers
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: A
OptionExplanation
A · A versioned data contract that specifies units and validates semantic expectationsSchema parsing checks structure; a contract must also describe the meaning and unit of amount.
B · Enable object versioning aloneVersioning preserves older objects but does not detect the changed business meaning.
C · Run the crawler more frequentlySchema inference can still see the same numeric type and miss the semantic change.
D · Increase Spark workersCompute capacity does not validate currency units.
CHAPTER 1 · Q3

A consumer writes an event to its destination, then crashes before recording its checkpoint. What design best protects the result after restart?

  1. Disable all retries
  2. Assume checkpoints prevent all duplicate writes
  3. Give each retry a new random event ID
  4. An idempotent sink write keyed by a stable business event ID
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: D
OptionExplanation
A · Disable all retriesAvoiding retries can lose work and does not provide a reliable recovery design.
B · Assume checkpoints prevent all duplicate writesThe failure occurred after the write and before the checkpoint.
C · Give each retry a new random event IDNew IDs make duplicate business events harder to recognize.
D · An idempotent sink write keyed by a stable business event IDThe replayed event carries the same logical ID, so a conditional or transactional sink operation can avoid duplicating its effect.
CHAPTER 1 · Q4

A phone records a sale yesterday but uploads it today. Revenue must be assigned to the time of sale. Which timestamp should drive the business window?

  1. The consumer's deployment timestamp
  2. Only the processing timestamp
  3. Event time, with a defined late-arrival policy
  4. The first time a dashboard refreshes
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: C
OptionExplanation
A · The consumer's deployment timestampDeployment time is unrelated to the sale.
B · Only the processing timestampProcessing time would assign the delayed sale to the wrong business interval.
C · Event time, with a defined late-arrival policyEvent time reflects the business action; late-event handling determines whether to update an earlier result.
D · The first time a dashboard refreshesDashboard refresh time does not establish when the source event occurred.
CHAPTER 1 · Q5

A distributed join leaves most workers idle while one task processes a dominant customer key. What should the engineer investigate first?

  1. TLS certificate renewal
  2. Data skew and the partition/join strategy
  3. Only total cluster worker count
  4. S3 bucket naming conventions
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: B
OptionExplanation
A · TLS certificate renewalA certificate issue would not explain one successful but extremely large join task.
B · Data skew and the partition/join strategyA hot key concentrates work; repartitioning, key treatment or a different join strategy may address the actual bottleneck.
C · Only total cluster worker countMore workers can remain idle if the same key still concentrates the work.
D · S3 bucket naming conventionsThe observed symptom concerns processing distribution, not naming.
CHAPTER 1 · Q6

A team must rebuild last month's curated results using corrected logic. Which design best enables a controlled rebuild?

  1. Keep only dashboard screenshots
  2. Delete raw files immediately after each successful run
  3. Overwrite all destinations without reconciliation
  4. Retain replayable raw inputs and record code versions, parameters and input scope
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: D
OptionExplanation
A · Keep only dashboard screenshotsScreenshots do not contain replayable source records.
B · Delete raw files immediately after each successful runThat removes the evidence needed to reproduce the transformation.
C · Overwrite all destinations without reconciliationUnvalidated replacement can introduce duplicates or loss beyond the intended interval.
D · Retain replayable raw inputs and record code versions, parameters and input scopeReproducible inputs and transformation metadata make the replay explainable and allow validation before replacement.
CHAPTER 1 · Q79

Which TWO design elements support a reliable replay after an interrupted pipeline?

  1. Retained source inputs
  2. Deletion of processing metadata
  3. Idempotent destination writes
  4. Random new business IDs on each retry
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: A, C
OptionExplanation
A · Retained source inputsInputs must still exist for the intended replay scope.
B · Deletion of processing metadataMetadata helps reproduce and investigate the run.
C · Idempotent destination writesRepeated input should not repeat its business effect.
D · Random new business IDs on each retryNew IDs can hide logical duplicates.
2. Batch ingestion, APIs & migration
DOMAIN 1 · TASKS 1.1, 2.1

Amazon S3 landing patterns

  • Use prefixes for source and arrival date
  • Track batch IDs and expected file counts
  • Separate incomplete uploads from publish-ready datasets
  • Record checksums and manifests where appropriate
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use a landing zone when many producers deliver files at different times.An object-created event is not a complete multi-file batch manifest.
Example & explanation
  • Publish a batch-ready marker after all expected export objects are available.
  • A completeness signal prevents downstream jobs from treating a partially delivered batch as the final dataset.

AWS DMS full load & CDC

  • Full load copies existing rows
  • CDC reads supported source change logs
  • Source permissions and log retention are prerequisites
  • Monitor source and target replication lag separately
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use full-load-and-CDC for a supported database migration with ongoing changes.DMS data replication does not convert every stored procedure or application query.
Example & explanation
  • Load an on-premises order database and keep the target synchronized until cutover.
  • Change capture reduces final migration downtime, but validation, engine-specific configuration and a controlled cutover remain necessary.

Schema conversion & validation

  • Homogeneous moves retain the database engine
  • Heterogeneous moves may require schema and code conversion
  • DMS Schema Conversion or SCT can assess supported objects
  • Validate totals, keys and critical queries
Choose / applyExam distinction
Run an assessment before committing to a migration design.A converted table definition does not certify identical application behavior.
Example & explanation
  • An Oracle-to-PostgreSQL move needs data type, function and procedural-code review.
  • Engine compatibility affects more than row transport. Testing representative business operations finds issues that row counts cannot.

AWS DataSync & Transfer Family

  • DataSync automates supported bulk transfers and verification
  • Transfer Family exposes managed file-transfer protocols
  • Both can land data in supported AWS storage
  • Choose based on the producer interface
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use DataSync for managed storage transfers; Transfer Family for partners requiring SFTP or another supported protocol.A protocol endpoint does not perform the downstream analytical transformation.
Example & explanation
  • A partner keeps its SFTP client while the platform lands files in S3.
  • Preserving a producer's contract can simplify integration. Transfer throughput, scheduling, permissions and downstream event handling are separate design choices.

Amazon AppFlow & API ingestion

  • AppFlow provides supported SaaS data connections
  • API integrations need pagination and incremental cursors
  • Respect provider quotas and token expiry
  • Persist the last successfully committed extraction point
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose managed connectors when the supported application and flow features fit.A successful first API response does not mean every page was extracted.
Example & explanation
  • Read all pages from a CRM API before marking the extraction interval complete.
  • Reliable API extraction needs state and reconciliation. Transient failures must resume without silently skipping a page or duplicating a whole interval.

JDBC, ODBC & private connectivity

  • Drivers connect processing engines to databases
  • JDBC URLs include the database and engine details
  • VPC routes, DNS and security groups must permit the path
  • Credentials belong in a managed secret
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use private connectivity and least-privilege database users for ingestion.IAM permission to start a Glue job does not open a network connection to RDS.
Example & explanation
  • A job with a valid password still fails if the database port is unreachable.
  • Connectivity, authentication and authorization are independent layers. Test them separately to avoid broadening permissions to solve a routing problem.

Rate limits, retries & backpressure

  • Bound request concurrency
  • Use exponential backoff with jitter
  • Retry transient errors with a finite budget
  • Buffer work when arrivals exceed processing capacity
Choose / applyExam distinction
Throttle producers or scale consumers while protecting the destination.Retrying every error immediately can create a retry storm.
Example & explanation
  • A CRM returns HTTP 429; delay and retry within the provider's quota instead of adding threads.
  • Backpressure keeps a downstream service from being overwhelmed. Monitoring queue age reveals when buffering is delaying the business outcome.

Events, schedules & batch completeness

  • S3 notifications react to object events
  • EventBridge routes matching events
  • EventBridge Scheduler initiates timed work
  • Use manifests or reconciliation for complete datasets
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use events for arrival-driven work and schedules for time-driven work.Notifications can be duplicated and out of order; make handlers idempotent.
Example & explanation
  • A scheduler checks for yesterday's manifest and starts the ETL only after completeness validation.
  • Triggers decide when to attempt work. The pipeline must independently verify that its prerequisites and inputs are valid.

Exercise: Publish an S3 batch manifest after successful uploads

  • Upload two source objects and publish a manifest only after both uploads succeed.
Setup
  • An existing private S3 lab bucket in your chosen Region.
  • AWS CLI v2 and a configured profile permitted to write/read the lab prefix.
  • Replace YOUR-UNIQUE-LAB-BUCKET and study with your own values.
Complete worked answer
  • Create the two local files and a manifest containing the expected object keys.
  • Use shell error handling so a failed upload prevents manifest publication.
  • Upload the files first and the manifest last.
  • A downstream job should read the manifest and verify the listed inputs before processing.
bash
set -eu
lab_bucket='YOUR-UNIQUE-LAB-BUCKET'
lab_profile='study'
printf 'order_id,amount\nA,10.50\n' > orders-1.csv
printf 'order_id,amount\nB,7.25\n' > orders-2.csv
cat > manifest.json <<'JSON'
{"batch_id":"b001","expected_count":2,"objects":[
 "raw/b001/orders-1.csv","raw/b001/orders-2.csv"]}
JSON
aws s3 cp orders-1.csv "s3://$lab_bucket/raw/b001/orders-1.csv" --profile "$lab_profile"
aws s3 cp orders-2.csv "s3://$lab_bucket/raw/b001/orders-2.csv" --profile "$lab_profile"
aws s3 cp manifest.json "s3://$lab_bucket/manifests/b001.json" --profile "$lab_profile"
aws s3 ls "s3://$lab_bucket/raw/b001/" --profile "$lab_profile"
aws s3 cp "s3://$lab_bucket/manifests/b001.json" - --profile "$lab_profile"

Expected result

  • The raw prefix contains both named CSV objects.
  • The manifest lists exactly those two keys; downstream validation still checks actual existence and integrity.

Why this works

  • The marker represents a logical batch boundary.
  • The example does not claim an atomic transaction across independent S3 objects; immutable batch IDs and validation make the handoff explicit.

Troubleshooting

  • If an upload fails, investigate profile, Region, IAM and key authorization before retrying.
  • Use a new batch ID for an independent test rather than accidentally mutating a published batch.

Cleanup

  • Remove only the three lab objects and local files you created; retain the bucket if it is shared.
CHAPTER 2 · Q7

A supported relational database must migrate while applications keep writing until cutover. Which DMS mode fits?

  1. A Glue crawler alone
  2. Full load with no ongoing replication
  3. Full load plus change data capture
  4. An S3 Lifecycle rule
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: C
OptionExplanation
A · A Glue crawler aloneA crawler discovers metadata; it does not maintain ongoing database replication.
B · Full load with no ongoing replicationNew writes after the initial copy would not remain synchronized.
C · Full load plus change data captureFull load transfers existing rows and CDC replicates subsequent source changes, with engine-specific prerequisites and validation.
D · An S3 Lifecycle ruleLifecycle manages object storage state, not source transaction changes.
CHAPTER 2 · Q8

An external partner must continue using SFTP to deliver files directly into the AWS landing solution. Which service is the closest fit?

  1. Amazon CloudWatch
  2. AWS DMS
  3. AWS Transfer Family with an appropriate supported storage target
  4. Amazon Athena
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: C
OptionExplanation
A · Amazon CloudWatchMonitoring does not provide the required SFTP interface.
B · AWS DMSDMS handles supported database replication rather than general partner SFTP uploads.
C · AWS Transfer Family with an appropriate supported storage targetTransfer Family provides managed protocol endpoints suited to a partner that retains an SFTP client.
D · Amazon AthenaAthena queries datasets and is not the requested file-transfer protocol endpoint.
CHAPTER 2 · Q9

A CRM API returns a continuation token and only part of the export. The script stores the first response and reports success. What is missing?

  1. A shorter column name
  2. Pagination through all responses plus a committed extraction checkpoint
  3. Additional EC2 memory only
  4. A wider destination bucket policy
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: B
OptionExplanation
A · A shorter column nameField naming does not retrieve omitted pages.
B · Pagination through all responses plus a committed extraction checkpointThe continuation token signals more data; a complete extraction must process all pages and record successful scope.
C · Additional EC2 memory onlyMemory does not cause the script to follow continuation tokens.
D · A wider destination bucket policyPermissions are not the stated failure when the first page already succeeds.
CHAPTER 2 · Q10

A private Glue job has correct database credentials but cannot connect to the database port. What should be checked next?

  1. Change every table to Parquet
  2. Routes, DNS and security-group access between the job and database
  3. Reset all bookmark state
  4. Give the job administrator access
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: B
OptionExplanation
A · Change every table to ParquetSerialization cannot repair a refused or unreachable connection.
B · Routes, DNS and security-group access between the job and databaseA valid identity does not establish network reachability; investigate the path independently.
C · Reset all bookmark stateBookmarks concern incremental progress rather than network access.
D · Give the job administrator accessBroad IAM permissions do not open a blocked database network path.
CHAPTER 2 · Q11

A producer delivers a nightly export as 50 objects. The first object event starts ETL and partial data is published. Which change best addresses the defect?

  1. Change the bucket's storage class
  2. Disable logging
  3. Start more jobs from the first event
  4. Require a batch-complete manifest or equivalent completeness check
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: D
OptionExplanation
A · Change the bucket's storage classStorage class does not tell the job whether all expected files arrived.
B · Disable loggingRemoving evidence does not repair publication correctness.
C · Start more jobs from the first eventParallel execution does not establish batch completeness.
D · Require a batch-complete manifest or equivalent completeness checkAn object event represents one arrival, not a guarantee that every object in the logical batch has been delivered.
CHAPTER 2 · Q12

A source API is returning 429 responses after the ingestion team increases concurrency. Which response is most appropriate?

  1. Bound concurrency and use backoff with jitter within the source's quota
  2. Treat 429 as proof of a bad schema
  3. Retry every failed request immediately on every thread
  4. Mark every throttled page as successfully extracted
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: A
OptionExplanation
A · Bound concurrency and use backoff with jitter within the source's quotaThe source is applying a rate limit; controlled retries and request pacing address it without amplifying overload.
B · Treat 429 as proof of a bad schemaThe response indicates request-rate handling, not necessarily record schema validity.
C · Retry every failed request immediately on every threadSynchronized aggressive retries can worsen the throttling.
D · Mark every throttled page as successfully extractedThat silently loses data.
CHAPTER 2 · Q80

Which TWO belong in a robust paginated API extraction?

  1. Assume every response is the full dataset
  2. Persist successfully committed extraction scope
  3. Follow continuation tokens
  4. Ignore rate-limit responses as successful pages
Answer & detailed explanationsAnswer: B, C
OptionExplanation
A · Assume every response is the full datasetMany APIs paginate their results.
B · Persist successfully committed extraction scopeA checkpoint supports correct continuation and reconciliation.
C · Follow continuation tokensTokens identify remaining pages.
D · Ignore rate-limit responses as successful pagesIgnoring failures silently loses data.
3. Streaming ingestion & processing
DOMAIN 1 · TASKS 1.1, 1.2

Kinesis Data Streams fundamentals

  • Producers write records using partition keys
  • Records are retained for replay within the configured retention window
  • Consumers track progress
  • Ordering is scoped to the relevant shard, not the entire stream
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose Kinesis for AWS-native retained event streams with independent consumers.Do not promise global ordering across all shards.
Example & explanation
  • Use device_id as a partition key when per-device event ordering matters.
  • A stream decouples producers from consumers while preserving a bounded history. The partition-key strategy determines both locality and load balance.

Capacity modes & hot partitions

  • Provisioned mode requires capacity planning
  • On-demand modes manage scaling behavior
  • Capacity changes are not a cure for unlimited hot-key concentration
  • Observe write throttling, consumer lag and distribution
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose a capacity model for the traffic profile and operational requirements.Average throughput hides spikes and single-key bottlenecks.
Example & explanation
  • Hash many distinct customer IDs rather than assigning every event the same partition key.
  • Balanced keys let the stream distribute work. A single overloaded partition can throttle while other capacity remains unused.

Shared throughput vs enhanced fan-out

  • Shared consumers contend for shard read capacity
  • Enhanced fan-out provides dedicated per-consumer read throughput
  • Independent consumer applications can progress separately
  • Additional isolation has a cost
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use enhanced fan-out when multiple low-latency consumers compete for reads.Adding polling consumers does not create unlimited shared read bandwidth.
Example & explanation
  • Fraud detection and live metrics each consume the same transaction stream without competing for shared read throughput.
  • Consumer isolation is valuable when one application's read behavior must not delay another. It does not remove destination or processing limits.

Amazon Data Firehose

  • Managed delivery buffers incoming data
  • Supported transformations and format conversion can be configured
  • Delivery writes to supported destinations
  • Error output and destination retries must be planned
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Firehose for managed delivery when buffering latency is acceptable.Firehose is not a general-purpose retained stream for arbitrary independent replay consumers.
Example & explanation
  • Deliver application events to partitioned S3 storage without operating a custom consumer fleet.
  • Managed delivery removes consumer infrastructure work. Destination configuration and buffering determine the freshness and layout of delivered data.

Amazon MSK & Kafka concepts

  • Kafka organizes records into topics and partitions
  • Consumer groups distribute partitions among members
  • Offsets record consumer progress
  • Schema compatibility is distinct from broker transport
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose MSK when Kafka APIs, connectors or ecosystem compatibility are requirements.More consumers than partitions do not necessarily increase group parallelism.
Example & explanation
  • A Kafka-based organization retains existing client libraries and consumer-group behavior on MSK.
  • Managed brokers reduce platform operations while leaving partition design, consumer behavior and application correctness in scope.

Flink windows, state & checkpoints

  • Managed Service for Apache Flink runs stateful stream applications
  • Windows aggregate bounded portions of events
  • Checkpoints capture recoverable processing state
  • Watermarks support event-time progress
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose Flink for continuous stateful joins or event-time aggregation.Engine recovery semantics do not automatically make every external sink exactly once.
Example & explanation
  • Calculate per-store five-minute revenue with a defined policy for late transactions.
  • Stateful processing requires coordinated recovery and bounded state. Sink integration and checkpoint configuration decide the practical end-to-end guarantee.

Lambda stream consumers

  • An event source mapping polls supported stream sources
  • Batches reduce invocation overhead
  • A failed batch can delay later processing
  • Failure controls and partial-batch responses need deliberate configuration
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Lambda for short event-driven transformations that fit its execution model.A poison record can block progress if retry handling is not designed.
Example & explanation
  • Isolate an invalid event, record its failure and continue supported processing rather than replaying the same batch forever.
  • Batch size, concurrency, record age and error handling together determine throughput and recovery behavior.

Replay & deduplication

  • Producer retries can create duplicate records
  • Consumer restarts can replay from a checkpoint
  • Business event IDs distinguish logical events
  • Retention must cover outage and catch-up time
Choose / applyExam distinction
Design consumers to tolerate repeats and measure lag against retention.A new sequence number does not prove the business event is new.
Example & explanation
  • A payment event is written twice after an acknowledgement timeout; deduplicate using payment_event_id.
  • Stream transport and business identity are different layers. Idempotent sinks make recovery safer even when the processing engine restarts successfully.

Exercise: Create a retained stream and publish a keyed event

  • Create an on-demand stream, send one order event using the order ID as the partition key, and inspect the stream.
Setup
  • AWS CLI v2; configured credentials with the relevant Kinesis permissions.
  • A chosen Region; creation can incur AWS charges.
  • The stream name must not collide with an existing resource.
Complete worked answer
  • Create the stream and wait for it to become active.
  • Send a small UTF-8 JSON payload using a stable business event ID.
  • Inspect the returned shard and sequence identifiers.
  • Explain why a retry still requires logical deduplication in the consumer.
bash
aws kinesis create-stream --stream-name dea-lab-events \
  --stream-mode-details StreamMode=ON_DEMAND --region us-east-1
aws kinesis wait stream-exists --stream-name dea-lab-events --region us-east-1
printf '{"event_id":"evt-001","order_id":"A","amount":10.50}' > event.json
aws kinesis put-record --stream-name dea-lab-events \
  --partition-key A --data fileb://event.json --region us-east-1
aws kinesis describe-stream-summary \
  --stream-name dea-lab-events --region us-east-1

Expected result

  • The put-record response includes ShardId and SequenceNumber.
  • The stream summary reports an active stream; this alone does not validate a downstream consumer.

Why this works

  • Partition keys control record placement.
  • Sequence numbers describe stream records; event_id describes the business event and is useful for duplicate handling.

Troubleshooting

  • Check Region, stream status and IAM if publication fails.
  • Do not use one constant key for all unrelated entities at production scale.

Cleanup

4. AWS Glue, Spark & transformation
DOMAIN 1 · TASKS 1.2, 1.4, 3.3

Glue job selection & worker sizing

  • Glue runs managed data integration jobs
  • Spark jobs distribute large transformations
  • Python-shell style workloads suit supported lighter tasks
  • Worker memory and parallelism should match the stages
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose the smallest effective execution model after profiling representative inputs.A tiny task does not require a distributed cluster simply because the data is in S3.
Example & explanation
  • A large join uses distributed Spark; a small metadata reconciliation may use a lightweight task.
  • Execution overhead, memory pressure and shuffle behavior often matter more than the raw row count.

DynamicFrame vs DataFrame

  • DynamicFrames help handle inconsistent semi-structured records
  • DataFrames use an explicit Spark schema
  • Conversions allow use of Spark SQL and DataFrame operations
  • Resolve ambiguous types before writing a strict target
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use explicit casts and error capture when source records disagree on types.An inferred string column does not establish valid business data.
Example & explanation
  • Cast amount to decimal and quarantine nonnumeric values before aggregation.
  • Schema decisions influence downstream correctness. Silently dropping failed casts can make a job look successful while losing revenue records.

Pushdown & partition pruning

  • Select only needed columns
  • Filter partitions before reading files
  • Glue push_down_predicate can prune supported catalog reads
  • Catalog partition indexes can reduce metadata lookup work
Choose / applyExam distinction
Reduce I/O early when the job needs a small date or tenant slice.Filtering after reading every object wastes scan and listing work.
Example & explanation
  • Read only business_date = 2026-10-01 rather than a complete multi-year archive.
  • Pushdown eliminates unnecessary work before transformation. Partition metadata, filter syntax and connector support determine whether the filter is effective.

Job bookmarks & incremental state

  • Bookmarks track supported source progress across successful runs
  • Stable transformation contexts identify tracked elements
  • Initialization and commit are part of the job lifecycle
  • Pause and reset change replay behavior
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use bookmarks for supported incremental reads, with an independent output strategy.Resetting a bookmark does not automatically delete previously written destination data.
Example & explanation
  • After replaying old S3 inputs, use deterministic partition replacement or upserts to avoid duplicates.
  • Bookmarks manage read progress. Output cleanup and exactly-once business effects are separate responsibilities.

Spark joins, shuffles & skew

  • Wide transformations redistribute data
  • Broadcasting a genuinely small dimension can avoid a large shuffle
  • Skew can overload a few tasks
  • Use execution plans and stage metrics
Choose / applyExam distinction
Optimize join strategy and data distribution before increasing worker count.Broadcasting a large relation can cause executor memory failures.
Example & explanation
  • Join a large fact dataset to a small, filtered reference table using a suitable broadcast strategy.
  • A balanced job can use all workers. A skewed join spends most of its time waiting for a few overloaded tasks.

Small files, compression & formats

  • Columnar Parquet or ORC supports analytical column selection
  • Compression reduces storage and I/O
  • Many tiny files increase planning and task overhead
  • Repartitioning and compaction improve output layout
Choose / applyExam distinction
Write query-friendly files and partitions rather than one object for each input event.One enormous output file can also reduce parallel reading.
Example & explanation
  • Compact thousands of tiny daily event files into a smaller set of balanced Parquet files.
  • The right file size depends on the engine and workload. Measure query planning, scan time and parallelism rather than assuming a universal target size.

EMR, containers & custom processing

  • EMR supports managed big-data processing frameworks
  • ECS or EKS suits packaged custom applications
  • Container images capture runtime dependencies
  • Choose resource shape, storage and scaling deliberately
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use EMR for Spark/Hadoop ecosystem requirements or containers for an existing packaged processor.Managed infrastructure does not eliminate dependency compatibility or application tuning.
Example & explanation
  • An organization with specialized Spark libraries chooses a compatible EMR runtime and tests the job before migration.
  • The service should match required frameworks and operational control. Portability still requires supported connectors, permissions and network paths.

LLMs in data processing

  • LLMs can classify or extract meaning from unstructured data
  • Require structured output validation
  • Track model, prompt and input versions
  • Handle throttling, cost, privacy and nondeterminism
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Bedrock-supported models for semantic extraction when deterministic parsing is inadequate.An LLM response is not automatically correct or safe to publish as a trusted record.
Example & explanation
  • Extract a document category, validate it against allowed labels, then route uncertain cases to review.
  • Language-model outputs need quality gates just like other transformations. Preserve evidence and use deterministic validation for fields with strict business rules.

Exercise: Transform CSV into validated Parquet with Glue Spark

  • Read CSV, validate/cast amount, write invalid rows to quarantine and valid rows to Parquet.
Setup
  • An existing Glue Spark job and execution role with access to the selected prefixes.
  • A raw CSV with headers order_id,amount; use the two CSV fixtures from Lab 2.
  • Pass job arguments --SOURCE and --TARGET as s3:// prefixes; TARGET must be an isolated lab prefix.
Complete worked answer
  • Set the input schema as strings so invalid values remain inspectable.
  • Cast to Decimal and explicitly separate rejected rows.
  • Write valid and invalid outputs to different paths.
  • Reconcile counts before deciding whether publication is permitted.
python
import sys
from awsglue.utils import getResolvedOptions
from pyspark.context import SparkContext
from awsglue.context import GlueContext
from awsglue.job import Job
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

args = getResolvedOptions(sys.argv, ["JOB_NAME", "SOURCE", "TARGET"])
glue = GlueContext(SparkContext.getOrCreate())
spark = glue.spark_session
job = Job(glue)
job.init(args["JOB_NAME"], args)
raw = (spark.read.option("header", True)
       .schema("order_id string, amount string").csv(args["SOURCE"]))
typed = raw.withColumn("amount_decimal",
    F.when(F.trim(F.col("amount")).rlike(r"^[0-9]{1,10}(\.[0-9]{1,2})?$"),
           F.trim(F.col("amount")).cast("decimal(12,2)")))
valid_condition = (F.col("order_id").isNotNull()
                   & (F.length(F.trim(F.col("order_id"))) > 0)
                   & F.col("amount_decimal").isNotNull()
                   & (F.col("amount_decimal") >= 0))
valid = typed.filter(valid_condition)
invalid = typed.filter(~F.coalesce(valid_condition, F.lit(False)))
valid.select("order_id", "amount_decimal").write.mode("errorifexists").parquet(
    args["TARGET"].rstrip("/") + "/valid/")
invalid.write.mode("errorifexists").json(args["TARGET"].rstrip("/") + "/quarantine/")
print({"input": raw.count(), "valid": valid.count(), "invalid": invalid.count()})
job.commit()

Expected result

  • For the two valid Lab 2 rows: input 2, valid 2, invalid 0.
  • The valid output is Parquet with a decimal amount column.
  • The example does not enable source bookmarks; independent reruns need a fresh target or a controlled replacement design.

Why this works

  • Validation and a separate quarantine path prevent silent row loss.
  • errorifexists deliberately refuses to append a replay to old outputs.
  • job.commit is present for the job lifecycle; it does not make arbitrary destination writes transactional.

Troubleshooting

  • Check source headers, prefixes, Glue runtime and role permissions.
  • The demonstration accepts nonnegative plain amounts with at most ten integer and two fractional digits; extend this explicit contract only when required.

Cleanup

  • Remove isolated lab output prefixes and stop/delete the lab job only if it was created for this exercise.

5. Orchestration & software engineering
DOMAIN 1 · TASKS 1.3, 1.4, 3.1

Step Functions workflow design

  • States express task dependencies and decisions
  • Parallel and Map states coordinate independent work
  • Service integrations can start and wait for supported jobs
  • Retries and catches express recovery paths
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use a managed state machine for explicit AWS-service orchestration.Starting an asynchronous job is not the same as waiting for its successful completion.
Example & explanation
  • Start a Glue job, wait for it, validate output, then publish the serving partition.
  • A workflow should advance only after the business prerequisite is satisfied. Status and output checks prevent a successful orchestration from publishing incomplete data.

MWAA & Airflow DAGs

  • Airflow models dependencies as a DAG
  • MWAA manages the Airflow environment
  • Tasks need idempotent behavior
  • Sensors, schedules and backfills influence resource use
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose MWAA for Airflow compatibility and a mature DAG/operator ecosystem.A DAG without a cycle can still contain incorrect business dependencies.
Example & explanation
  • Make warehouse publication depend on both source ingestion and quality validation.
  • Task graphs encode ordering, not correctness. Network access, environment dependencies and external service credentials still require management.

Glue workflows & EventBridge

  • Glue workflows coordinate Glue-oriented components
  • Triggers express scheduled or conditional starts
  • EventBridge routes service and application events
  • Scheduling and transformation are separate concerns
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Glue-native orchestration for a primarily Glue pipeline.An event bus does not transform all records in the data plane.
Example & explanation
  • An arrival event initiates a workflow that crawls, transforms and validates a new dataset.
  • Control-plane events initiate work; the bulk data path should remain in the appropriate storage and processing services.

Retries, timeouts & compensation

  • Retry transient failures with bounded backoff
  • Timeout stalled operations
  • Route unrecoverable inputs to quarantine
  • Compensate for partially completed external actions where needed
Choose / applyExam distinction
Define retries according to operation semantics and failure type.Retrying an invalid schema forever will not repair the data.
Example & explanation
  • A timed-out API write is retried with the same idempotency key.
  • Recovery must account for uncertain success. Repeating side effects without a stable key can introduce duplicate business actions.

Python, SDKs & pagination

  • Use SDK paginators for multi-page APIs
  • Stream large inputs rather than loading everything into memory
  • Validate configuration and input types
  • Log identifiers and counts without leaking sensitive payloads
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use structured functions with testable boundaries for cloud calls and transformation logic.A list API call commonly returns only one page.
Example & explanation
  • Iterate a Glue get_tables paginator to inspect the complete database catalog.
  • Correct small scripts still need pagination, error handling and controlled memory use when production datasets grow.

SQL & algorithmic efficiency

  • Push aggregations into an appropriate query engine
  • Filter early
  • Use keyed lookups instead of repeated full scans
  • Understand time and memory complexity
Choose / applyExam distinction
Compare execution plans and data movement when optimizing code.A nested Python loop over two large datasets is not equivalent to an indexed or distributed join.
Example & explanation
  • Replace repeated list membership checks with a set when memory and key semantics permit.
  • Algorithm choice affects runtime even before AWS capacity is considered. Distributed execution adds communication and serialization costs.

IaC, SAM & CI/CD

  • CloudFormation and CDK define repeatable infrastructure
  • SAM simplifies supported serverless packaging
  • CI tests changes before deployment
  • Separate environment-specific parameters and secrets
Choose / applyExam distinction
Version jobs, schemas, policies and infrastructure together.A successful deployment is not a successful data migration or backfill.
Example & explanation
  • Deploy the same pipeline definition with different test and production bucket parameters.
  • Repeatable delivery reduces configuration drift. Data contracts and rollback procedures must accompany code changes.

Testing, storage & Lambda concurrency

  • Unit-test transformations with edge cases
  • Integration-test permissions and service boundaries
  • Lambda /tmp is temporary execution storage
  • EFS integration requires a supported VPC setup
  • Reserved concurrency can protect a downstream database
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use concurrency controls to prevent invocation bursts from exhausting destination connections.Increasing concurrency can make a database bottleneck worse.
Example & explanation
  • Process test records with nulls, duplicate keys and malformed timestamps before increasing throughput.
  • Performance and correctness tests answer different questions. A pipeline needs both, plus a plan for temporary files and state persistence.

Exercise: Orchestrate transform → quality gate → publish

  • Wait for transformation, run validation and permit publication only when the quality result is true.
Setup
  • An existing Glue job and quality-check Lambda function.
  • The Lambda returns an object such as {"passed": true}.
  • A state-machine role permitted to use the relevant integrations; replace account and resource placeholders.
Complete worked answer
  • Use the supported Glue .sync integration so transformation completes before the next state.
  • Invoke the quality function and retain its response.
  • Use a Choice state against the actual returned payload shape.
  • Use a failure state when quality is false; replace the final Pass with your controlled publication action.
json
{
  "StartAt": "Transform",
  "States": {
    "Transform": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::glue:startJobRun.sync",
      "Parameters": {"JobName": "YOUR_GLUE_JOB"},
      "ResultPath": "$.transform",
      "Catch": [{"ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "Next": "Failed"}],
      "Next": "Validate"
    },
    "Validate": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {
        "FunctionName": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:YOUR_CHECK",
        "Payload.$": "$"
      },
      "ResultPath": "$.quality",
      "Catch": [{"ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "Next": "Failed"}],
      "Next": "QualityPassed"
    },
    "QualityPassed": {
      "Type": "Choice",
      "Choices": [{"Variable": "$.quality.Payload.passed", "BooleanEquals": true,
                   "Next": "ReadyToPublish"}],
      "Default": "Failed"
    },
    "ReadyToPublish": {"Type": "Pass", "End": true},
    "Failed": {"Type": "Fail", "Error": "PipelineOrQualityFailure"}
  }
}

Expected result

  • A Glue failure cannot advance to quality publication.
  • A false quality response leads to Failed.
  • A true response reaches ReadyToPublish, which is intentionally a study placeholder rather than a data publication implementation.

Why this works

  • The control flow makes dependencies explicit.
  • A successful Lambda invocation is different from the function reporting that data quality passed.

Troubleshooting

  • A wrong JSON path can make the quality decision fail.
  • Use a Standard workflow when relying on the supported .sync job integration and verify the integration execution-role permissions.

Cleanup

  • Remove any lab-only state machine and associated test execution resources after retaining study notes.

6. S3 lakes, catalogs & lifecycle
DOMAIN 2 · TASKS 2.1, 2.2, 2.3

S3 objects & lake zones

  • S3 stores objects addressed by bucket and key
  • Prefixes are naming structures rather than physical directories
  • Raw, curated and serving zones separate responsibilities
  • Strong object consistency does not create multi-object transactions
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use S3 for a durable analytical lake with independent processing engines.A group of object writes is not automatically one atomic dataset commit.
Example & explanation
  • Publish a manifest or use a transactional table format when readers require a consistent multi-file snapshot.
  • Object durability, access controls and dataset-level consistency are different properties.

Glue Data Catalog & crawlers

  • The catalog stores technical table and partition metadata
  • Crawlers can infer supported schemas
  • Tables point to source locations
  • Schemas can also be defined and updated explicitly
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use a shared technical catalog so Athena, Glue and other compatible engines agree on metadata.A crawler does not move source files into the catalog.
Example & explanation
  • Catalog a Parquet prefix and query its table through Athena.
  • Metadata connects an engine's logical schema to physical files. It must stay aligned with layout, serialization and producer changes.

Partitions, indexes & projection

  • Partitions can reduce data scanned
  • Register partitions or use supported projection rules
  • Catalog partition indexes accelerate suitable metadata filters
  • Choose partition granularity using actual query predicates
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use date or another useful low-to-moderate cardinality key when most queries filter by it.Partitioning by a unique identifier can create excessive tiny partitions.
Example & explanation
  • Daily date partitions support daily reports better than a separate partition for every order.
  • Pruning saves work only when the query and physical layout align. Too many partitions can move the bottleneck to metadata planning.

Parquet, ORC, CSV & Avro

  • CSV is simple but weakly typed
  • Parquet and ORC are columnar
  • Avro supports row-oriented serialization with schema
  • Choose compression supported by the intended engines
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use columnar formats for repeated analytical scans over selected fields.Changing a filename suffix does not convert the serialization format.
Example & explanation
  • Write Parquet using a transformation job or CTAS and compare bytes scanned for the same query.
  • Format conversion changes physical encoding. Schema, compression and partition layout together determine analytical efficiency.

S3 Lifecycle & archive retrieval

  • Lifecycle transitions objects between configured storage classes
  • Expiration removes eligible objects
  • Archived classes can require restoration before access
  • Minimum durations and retrieval behavior affect cost
Choose / applyExam distinction
Match classes to access frequency, recovery time and retention requirements.The lowest storage price may create unacceptable query or restore latency.
Example & explanation
  • Keep recent queryable data online and archive older raw evidence only when restoration delay is acceptable.
  • Storage optimization includes retrieval, transition and request costs. Query engines need access to the actual object bytes.

Versioning, Object Lock & deletion

  • Versioning retains multiple object versions
  • Delete markers can hide a current version
  • Object Lock enforces supported retention or legal holds
  • Noncurrent versions need lifecycle rules too
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use retention controls when immutable evidence is required.An ordinary delete does not necessarily erase every historical version.
Example & explanation
  • A privacy deletion workflow inventories versions, replicas and derived copies before reporting completion.
  • Business deletion requirements can conflict with legal retention. The pipeline must apply the agreed policy across all copies, not just the visible current object.

DynamoDB TTL & backup retention

  • TTL uses an epoch-seconds attribute
  • Expired items are removed asynchronously
  • Reads may still see expired items until deletion
  • Backup and export copies have independent lifecycles
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use TTL for automatic eventual expiry, with application filtering where needed.TTL is not an exact-second deletion guarantee.
Example & explanation
  • Exclude expired sessions in the application while DynamoDB removes them in the background.
  • Operational expiry and legally required deletion have different timing and evidence needs.

Technical vs business catalogs

  • A technical catalog describes locations, columns and partitions
  • A business catalog adds ownership, terms and discoverability
  • Lineage explains origin and transformation
  • Discovery must be paired with actual data authorization
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Glue metadata for query engines and SageMaker Catalog for governed business discovery where appropriate.Seeing an asset in a catalog does not necessarily grant permission to read its data.
Example & explanation
  • An analyst finds a dataset by a business glossary term, requests access, then queries the approved table.
  • Discovery, approval and enforcement are separate steps in governed data consumption.

Exercise: Catalog a CSV source and query it in Athena

  • Define a technical table and confirm the complete batch contains two rows with total amount 17.75.
Setup
  • Lab 2 files in an isolated S3 prefix.
  • An Athena workgroup with an allowed query-result location and suitable permissions.
  • The fixture has no quoted commas; this simple CSV definition is only for that fixture.
Complete worked answer
  • Create the database and the external table.
  • Use string fields so invalid amounts can be inspected.
  • Query the batch and compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(amount).
  • If production CSV includes quoted delimiters, use a suitable SerDe rather than assuming this simple delimiter definition is sufficient.
sql
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dea_lab;

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dea_lab.orders_raw (
  order_id string,
  amount string
)
ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','
STORED AS TEXTFILE
LOCATION 's3://YOUR-UNIQUE-LAB-BUCKET/raw/b001/'
TBLPROPERTIES ('skip.header.line.count'='1');

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_seen,
       SUM(TRY_CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(12,2))) AS total_amount
FROM dea_lab.orders_raw;

Expected result

  • rows_seen = 2; total_amount = 17.75 for the embedded Lab 2 fixture.
  • The catalog table points to the files; it does not copy them into a database.

Why this works

  • A table definition connects storage layout with an engine schema.
  • TRY_CAST avoids aborting this exploratory query on an invalid amount, but production must separately count and handle failed conversions.

Troubleshooting

  • Access denied can involve workgroup, catalog, source S3, result S3 or KMS permissions.
  • Wrong delimiters or source paths can produce misleading rows without a network error.

Cleanup

  • Drop the external table/database only if created for the lab. Remove lab query-result objects separately; dropping an ordinary external table does not erase the source files.

7. Redshift warehouses & modeling
DOMAIN 2 · TASKS 2.1, 2.4, 3.2

Warehouse vs operational database

  • Redshift targets analytical processing
  • RDS and Aurora target relational application workloads
  • Columnar analytical layouts favor scans and aggregation
  • Choose workload isolation and scaling requirements explicitly
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Redshift for warehouse analytics across large structured datasets.A high-volume transaction application is not automatically a warehouse workload.
Example & explanation
  • Keep checkout transactions in an operational database and analyze historical sales in Redshift.
  • Service selection follows access pattern, concurrency and latency. Separating analytical scans can protect the operational system.

Star schemas & fact grain

  • Facts represent measurable events at a defined grain
  • Dimensions describe entities and context
  • Surrogate keys support dimension history
  • Document additive, semi-additive and nonadditive measures
Choose / applyExam distinction
Define the grain before designing keys and aggregation logic.Joining facts to duplicate dimension keys can inflate metrics.
Example & explanation
  • A fact row represents one order line, not both an entire order and an item summary.
  • Consistent grain prevents double counting. A dimensional model should match the questions analysts need to answer.

Distribution & join movement

  • Distribution determines row placement across compute resources
  • A suitable common join key can reduce redistribution
  • ALL can help appropriate small dimensions at extra storage cost
  • AUTO lets supported automatic optimization choose
Choose / applyExam distinction
Inspect query plans and filtered data sizes when tuning joins.A low-cardinality or skewed distribution key can concentrate work.
Example & explanation
  • Co-locate a large fact table with an important dimension on an appropriate shared key.
  • The goal is balanced work with less network movement. A frequently used key is useful only if its distribution and filtered workload also fit.

Sort keys, compression & maintenance

  • Sort order can help selective range scans
  • Compression reduces storage and I/O
  • Statistics inform the optimizer
  • Automatic optimization and maintenance should be understood before manual changes
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use observed filters and plans to assess physical design.A sort key and a distribution key solve different problems.
Example & explanation
  • Date-filtered reporting may benefit from a useful sort strategy even when joins use a customer distribution key.
  • Row placement affects joins; ordering affects block skipping. Statistics and layout must reflect the data after significant changes.

COPY, staging & MERGE

  • COPY loads supported sources efficiently
  • Stage incoming records before validation
  • MERGE supports supported match-based updates and inserts
  • Deduplicate source keys before applying changes
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use staged set-based loads instead of row-at-a-time API inserts for large batches.A successful load does not prove uniqueness or reconciliation.
Example & explanation
  • Load a daily change file to staging, select one row per key, then merge into the target.
  • Staging separates arrival from publication. It supports quarantine, reconciliation and restart without partially publishing an unvalidated batch.

UNLOAD, Spectrum & federated access

  • UNLOAD exports query results to S3
  • Spectrum queries compatible external lake data
  • Federated queries access supported external operational sources
  • Data movement and source load still affect performance
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use the method that matches ownership, freshness and storage requirements.External querying does not make every remote query free or fast.
Example & explanation
  • Join a warehouse dimension with historical lake data rather than loading every archive partition into Redshift first.
  • Remote access can reduce duplication but introduces data-source performance, networking and authorization dependencies.

Workload management & materialization

  • Workload management controls query resource behavior
  • Materialized views persist supported query results
  • Refresh policies determine freshness
  • Serverless and provisioned options change operations and capacity choices
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use materialized views for repeated expensive aggregates when refresh semantics fit.A cached aggregate can be fast and still be too stale for the business question.
Example & explanation
  • Refresh a daily revenue aggregate after the corresponding validated batch is published.
  • Performance optimization must preserve freshness and correctness. Query isolation helps prevent one workload from starving another.

Locks, transactions & data sharing

  • Transactions group related changes
  • Locks can block concurrent work
  • Keep transactions scoped and inspect blockers
  • Supported Redshift sharing can expose data without a separate ETL copy
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use database privileges and transaction design in addition to IAM controls.IAM permission to connect does not grant every SQL privilege.
Example & explanation
  • A long-running transaction holds a lock while a load waits; inspect and resolve the blocker rather than simply increasing compute.
  • Database coordination and authorization remain important in a managed warehouse. Diagnose waits before treating every delay as a capacity problem.

Exercise: Stage and deterministically merge customer updates

  • Apply the newest update per customer key without retaining two current rows.
Setup
  • An existing Redshift database/session with permission to create temporary tables.
  • No external data file is required; the fixture is embedded.
Complete worked answer
  • Create a current-state table and a staging table.
  • Insert two updates for customer A with different source sequence values.
  • Use ROW_NUMBER with a deterministic tie-breaker to select one update per key.
  • MERGE the deduplicated staging set and inspect the target.
sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE lab_current (customer_id VARCHAR(20), status VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO lab_current VALUES ('A', 'old');
CREATE TEMP TABLE lab_stage (
  customer_id VARCHAR(20), status VARCHAR(20), source_seq BIGINT);
INSERT INTO lab_stage VALUES ('A','silver',1), ('A','gold',2), ('B','new',1);
CREATE TEMP TABLE lab_dedup AS
SELECT customer_id, status
FROM lab_stage AS s
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
  PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY source_seq DESC) = 1;
MERGE INTO lab_current
USING lab_dedup
ON lab_current.customer_id = lab_dedup.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET status = lab_dedup.status
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id,status)
VALUES (lab_dedup.customer_id,lab_dedup.status);
SELECT * FROM lab_current ORDER BY customer_id;

Expected result

  • Two current rows: A → gold; B → new.
  • The input change count is three, but the current-state output grain is one row per customer.

Why this works

  • Deduplication creates a single intended source match for each target key.
  • The correct count is determined by the current-state grain, not by blindly preserving every input change as another current row.

Troubleshooting

  • If sequence values tie, add a stable further tie-breaker according to the data contract.
  • Check transaction scope and concurrent writers before applying this pattern to production.

Cleanup

  • Temporary tables end with the session; drop them explicitly if you keep the session open.

An operations team sees a load waiting for a long transaction's lock. What should it do first?

B · Identify and resolve the blocking transaction according to the runbookThe symptom is a database coordination wait, so diagnose the blocker before treating it as a compute shortage.

CHAPTER 7 · Q42

The same expensive sales aggregation serves many repeated queries and can refresh after each validated daily load. What optimization fits?

  1. An unbounded retry policy

CHAPTER 7 · Q85

Which TWO help prevent incorrect warehouse aggregates?

8. Operational stores, Iceberg & vectors
DOMAIN 2 · TASKS 2.1, 2.4

DynamoDB keys & indexes

  • A partition key distributes items
  • A sort key orders related items within a partition-key value
  • Secondary indexes support alternate access patterns
  • Query is key-driven; Scan reads broadly
Choose / applyExam distinction
Design keys from known access patterns before creating indexes.An index is not a substitute for a poor partition-key distribution.
Example & explanation
  • Query a tenant's events using tenant_id plus an event-time sort key.
  • Predictable key access supports scalable reads. Hot tenants and large item collections still need deliberate design.

RDS, Aurora & connection patterns

  • Relational engines support joins and transactions
  • Indexes trade write cost for selective reads
  • Connection limits can bottleneck serverless clients
  • Read replicas and availability configurations serve different needs
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use a relational store when relational constraints and transaction semantics matter.A read replica is not interchangeable with every failover standby.
Example & explanation
  • Use a suitable proxy or connection-pooling pattern for bursts of short-lived clients.
  • Managed infrastructure reduces operations but does not redesign SQL, indexes or client connection behavior.

MemoryDB & specialist stores

  • MemoryDB offers durable in-memory database capabilities
  • Neptune targets graph relationships
  • DocumentDB targets compatible document workloads
  • OpenSearch targets search and analysis patterns
Choose / applyExam distinction
Select the data model and durability requirement before comparing brand names.A graph traversal workload is not automatically a good relational join design at the required scale.
Example & explanation
  • Use graph relationships for multi-hop connections and key/value access for low-latency keyed state.
  • Specialized engines optimize different operations. Feature compatibility and operational constraints must be tested for the actual client and workload.

Iceberg table structure & snapshots

  • Iceberg is an open table format above physical data files
  • Metadata tracks snapshots and referenced files
  • Supported engines can perform transactional table operations
  • Schema and partition evolution reduce disruptive rewrites
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Iceberg when lake tables need table-level commits, evolution or time travel.Parquet is a file format; Iceberg is a table format that can manage Parquet files.
Example & explanation
  • A reader selects a consistent table snapshot while another job commits an update.
  • A table format coordinates metadata and file sets so readers do not simply list arbitrary objects as one dataset.

Iceberg maintenance & S3 Tables

  • Compaction rewrites small or fragmented files
  • Snapshot expiry limits historical recovery
  • Orphan cleanup removes eligible unreferenced objects
  • S3 Tables provides managed table-storage capabilities for supported use cases
Choose / applyExam distinction
Plan table maintenance and retention together.Deleting files directly from an Iceberg location can break referenced snapshots.
Example & explanation
  • Run supported compaction and vacuum operations with a retention policy that preserves required history.
  • Transactional metadata does not eliminate storage growth. Cleanup must respect snapshot references and engine-specific behavior.

Schema evolution & compatibility

  • Adding an optional field can be compatible
  • Renaming or changing types can break consumers
  • Table formats and engines support different evolution rules
  • Version contracts and test downstream readers
Choose / applyExam distinction
Plan schema migration across producers, catalogs, jobs and consumers.A crawler updating a schema does not update every transformation and dashboard.
Example & explanation
  • Add a nullable source field, update tested transformations, then migrate consumers before removing an old field.
  • Schema change is a coordinated delivery problem. Physical compatibility and business meaning both matter.

Embeddings, chunks & retrieval

  • Embeddings encode content into numerical vectors
  • Chunking affects retrieval context and index size
  • Metadata filters narrow eligible results
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases can coordinate supported ingestion and retrieval
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use vector retrieval for semantic similarity, with source provenance and authorization.Similarity is not factual verification or access-control enforcement.
Example & explanation
  • Retrieve policy passages using an embedding of the user's question before generating a response.
  • Retrieval quality depends on source preparation, chunk boundaries, embedding compatibility and the chosen similarity measure.

HNSW vs IVF indexes

  • HNSW uses a navigable graph structure for approximate search
  • IVF narrows search to selected vector clusters
  • Recall, latency, memory and build work trade off
  • Embedding dimension and distance metric must match the index
Choose / applyExam distinction
Benchmark representative retrieval queries and required recall.Changing embedding models can require re-embedding and rebuilding the index.
Example & explanation
  • Compare index recall and latency on a labeled validation set instead of selecting by name alone.
  • Approximate search exchanges exhaustive comparison for efficient candidate discovery. The best configuration depends on dataset size, update pattern and accuracy needs.

Exercise: Create and maintain a small Iceberg table

  • Create an Iceberg table, insert two records and understand the effect of compaction versus snapshot cleanup.
Setup
  • An Athena engine 3 workgroup and isolated S3 table location.
  • Relevant Glue catalog, S3 and key permissions.
  • Use a fresh location and retain snapshots needed for the exercise.
Complete worked answer
  • Create the table using the Iceberg table properties.
  • Insert the fixture and verify the count and total.
  • Study OPTIMIZE as file-layout maintenance.
  • Study VACUUM as snapshot/orphan cleanup; run it only with an intentional retention configuration.
sql
CREATE TABLE dea_lab.orders_iceberg (
  order_id string,
  amount decimal(12,2)
)
LOCATION 's3://YOUR-UNIQUE-LAB-BUCKET/iceberg/orders/'
TBLPROPERTIES ('table_type'='ICEBERG', 'format'='parquet');

INSERT INTO dea_lab.orders_iceberg VALUES
  ('A', DECIMAL '10.50'), ('B', DECIMAL '7.25');
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_seen, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM dea_lab.orders_iceberg;

-- Maintenance examples; choose retention and timing deliberately.
OPTIMIZE dea_lab.orders_iceberg REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK;
-- VACUUM dea_lab.orders_iceberg;

Expected result

  • rows_seen = 2 and total_amount = 17.75 after one insert.
  • Compaction can change physical files without changing those business results.
  • Expired snapshots are no longer available for historical time travel.

Why this works

  • Iceberg metadata coordinates committed snapshots over physical data files.
  • Compaction and retention solve different maintenance problems.

Troubleshooting

  • Do not add ordinary external-table assumptions blindly to an Iceberg definition.
  • Do not remove referenced files manually from S3 while the table remains in use.

Cleanup

  • Use the engine/table-format cleanup procedure for a disposable table and confirm remaining lab storage. Keep shared datasets untouched.

A lake table requires consistent snapshots, schema evolution and supported row-level updates. What capability best addresses these table-level needs?

  1. An open table format such as Apache Iceberg, used through compatible engines

  4. Only an S3 prefix naming standard

OptionExplanation
A · An open table format such as Apache Iceberg, used through compatible enginesIceberg coordinates table metadata and file snapshots above physical files, unlike a file format alone.
B · Only a .parquet filename extensionFile encoding and naming do not provide the required table transaction metadata.
C · Only object compressionCompression reduces bytes but does not implement table evolution or updates.
D · Only an S3 prefix naming standardPrefixes alone do not coordinate snapshots and commits.

An engineer needs to remove unreferenced files and expire old snapshots in an Athena Iceberg table. Which operation fits?

  1. Delete arbitrary data files directly from S3
  2. Change the dataset's display title
  3. Supported VACUUM maintenance with a deliberate retention policy
  4. Run a SELECT * query repeatedly

A · Delete arbitrary data files directly from S3That can remove files still referenced by valid snapshots.
B · Change the dataset's display titleBusiness metadata does not clean physical table files.
C · Supported VACUUM maintenance with a deliberate retention policyVacuum can expire snapshots and remove eligible orphan files, which also affects available historical time travel.
D · Run a SELECT * query repeatedlyReading a table does not perform the requested cleanup.
CHAPTER 8 · Q45

A Bedrock retrieval system changes its embedding model to one with a different vector dimension. What should be planned?

A · Keep old vectors and compare them blindly with the new dimensionThe representations are incompatible.
