9. SQL, Athena & analytical optimization
DOMAIN 3 · TASKS 3.1, 3.2

Athena queries & workgroups

  • Athena queries supported data with managed compute
  • Workgroups separate configuration and usage controls
  • Result locations and encryption need configuration
  • Source data and result data both require permissions
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use Athena for SQL over compatible lake datasets without managing a warehouse cluster.A workgroup does not by itself grant access to S3 or a KMS key.
Example & explanation
  • A reporting team uses a controlled workgroup with an encrypted results prefix.
  • Engine configuration, data authorization and query correctness are separate layers.

Partition pruning & bytes scanned

  • Filter on useful partition columns
  • Select only needed data columns
  • Use columnar storage and compatible predicates
  • Compare scan metrics before and after a change
Choose / applyExam distinction
Tune file layout and predicates when scan cost dominates.Adding a LIMIT does not guarantee proportionate scan reduction.
Example & explanation
  • A date-filtered query over date-partitioned Parquet scans less irrelevant data than SELECT * over raw CSV.
  • The optimizer can skip only what the physical layout and predicates expose. Measure the actual plan and scanned bytes.

CTAS, views & reusable outputs

  • CTAS materializes a query result as a new table
  • A normal view stores a query definition
  • Materialized outputs have their own freshness and cleanup needs
  • Choose unique output locations for reproducible jobs
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use CTAS for format conversion and curated analytical datasets when its constraints fit.A view is not necessarily a cached or stored result.
Example & explanation
  • Create a Parquet daily-sales table from validated raw rows using a fresh target prefix.
  • Materialization trades storage and refresh work for faster reuse. A plain view still executes underlying query logic.

Joins, nulls & cardinality

  • Join type determines which unmatched rows survive
  • Null comparisons need explicit handling
  • Repeated join keys can multiply rows
  • Preaggregate or deduplicate when required by the grain
Choose / applyExam distinction
Check row counts and business totals at each join boundary.COUNT(column) does not count null values, unlike COUNT(*).
Example & explanation
  • A left join followed by a right-table WHERE predicate can accidentally discard unmatched rows.
  • Query syntax can subtly change business meaning. Correct joins depend on grain and uniqueness as well as available compute.

Window functions & ranking

  • PARTITION BY defines groups without collapsing rows
  • ORDER BY defines sequence within each group
  • ROW_NUMBER can select a deterministic latest row
  • Explicit window frames define rolling calculations
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use windows for latest-record selection, running totals and rankings.A row-based frame and a time-based business window are not always equivalent.
Example & explanation
  • Order by event_time and an ingestion tie-breaker when selecting the latest customer update.
  • Deterministic ordering avoids unstable results when timestamps tie. Late events can change historical aggregates and require a correction policy.

Aggregation, pivoting & reconciliation

  • GROUP BY changes the result grain
  • Conditional aggregation can pivot known categories
  • Distinct counts answer a different question from total events
  • Reconcile raw, valid and rejected counts
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use an explicit measure definition for each reporting metric.Averaging averages can misweight groups of different sizes.
Example & explanation
  • Compute total revenue divided by total orders instead of the unweighted average of regional averages.
  • Correct aggregation preserves the intended denominator and data grain. Reconciliation catches silent loss and duplication.

Notebooks, DataBrew & preparation

  • Notebooks support interactive exploration
  • Athena Spark notebooks use a different execution path from Athena SQL
  • DataBrew provides supported visual preparation recipes
  • Production transformations need versioned, reproducible logic
Choose / applyExam distinction
Explore with notebooks, then operationalize validated transformations.An interactive successful cell sequence is not a reliable scheduled pipeline.
Example & explanation
  • A profiling notebook identifies inconsistent date formats, then a tested job standardizes them.
  • Exploration finds patterns and defects. Production needs repeatable dependencies, inputs, permissions and error handling.

BI, QuickSight & freshness

  • Dashboards consume prepared data
  • Direct query and imported acceleration have different freshness behavior
  • Row-level controls must match the intended audience
  • Refresh after validated publication
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose a dashboard access mode according to latency, concurrency and freshness.A current dashboard timestamp does not prove every upstream batch was complete.
Example & explanation
  • Refresh a daily dataset after the quality gate and expose the data's business-date watermark.
  • Business consumers need freshness evidence and correct authorization, not just a responsive visualization.

Exercise: Deduplicate with a window and reconcile totals

  • Choose the latest row per order using timestamp and ingestion sequence, then calculate the resulting total.
Setup
  • An Athena SQL query editor; no source table is required.
Complete worked answer
  • Run the self-contained VALUES fixture.
  • Rank rows within each order_id.
  • Keep only the rank-one row using the defined timestamp and sequence ordering.
  • Compare raw event count to the final current-state order count.
sql
WITH events(order_id, event_time, ingestion_seq, amount) AS (
  VALUES
    ('A', TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 10:00:00', 1, DECIMAL '10.00'),
    ('A', TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 10:00:00', 2, DECIMAL '12.00'),
    ('B', TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 10:05:00', 1, DECIMAL '11.00')
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_time DESC, ingestion_seq DESC) AS rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS current_orders, SUM(amount) AS current_amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

Expected result

  • current_orders = 2; current_amount = 23.00.
  • A resolves to amount 12.00 because ingestion_seq breaks the timestamp tie.

Why this works

  • A deterministic tie-breaker makes repeated execution reproducible.
  • The output is current-state data, so summing all three source rows would answer the wrong question.

Troubleshooting

  • Without the secondary ordering key, timestamp ties do not establish the intended winner.
  • Do not treat a row-count change caused by intentional deduplication as unexplained data loss; document the grain.

Cleanup

  • No source table is created. Remove disposable Athena result objects if desired.

An Athena query reads only two needed fields for one date but scans a large raw CSV history. Which combined change is most promising?

  4. Convert to columnar data and align date partitioning with query predicates

OptionExplanation
A · Rename the columns without rewriting the dataNames do not create columnar encoding or partitions.
B · Store credentials in the query textThat adds risk without improving the access pattern.
C · Add LIMIT 10 and assume almost no data is scannedLIMIT does not guarantee the intended scan reduction.
D · Convert to columnar data and align date partitioning with query predicatesColumn selection and partition pruning can reduce unnecessary I/O when the physical layout supports them.
CHAPTER 9 · Q50

A query must retain customers with no orders, but a WHERE predicate on the right-hand order table removes them after a LEFT JOIN. What is the issue?

  1. The database must have ignored the join entirely

A · The database must have ignored the join entirelyThe symptom is consistent with normal null and predicate behavior.
B · The post-join predicate rejects unmatched null rowsThe predicate can effectively remove the unmatched rows the left join was intended to preserve; place and design conditions according to the required semantics.
C · S3 cannot store customers without ordersThe defect is in query logic, not object storage.
D · Encryption always converts unmatched values to zeroThat is not the described SQL behavior.

  2. 100 and 88
  3. 88 and 88
  4. 100 and 100

A · 88 and 100The roles of the two expressions are reversed.
B · 100 and 88COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(amount) counts rows where amount is non-null.
C · 88 and 88COUNT(*) does not exclude a row simply because one field is null.
D · 100 and 100COUNT(amount) excludes the null values.

A · Assume identical timestamps prove identical recordsDifferent updates can share a timestamp.
B · Omit ORDER BY completelyThat does not define latest or deterministic ordering.
C · A deterministic secondary ordering key in addition to event timeA stable tie-breaker defines which otherwise tied row wins.
D · Use a fresh random number as the only ordering keyThat changes the winner unpredictably.

B · The unweighted average of regional average order valuesThat can over-weight small regions.

Which TWO are valid SQL correctness checks?

B · Handle null comparisons deliberatelyNull behavior affects filters and aggregates.

10. Operations, monitoring & cost
DOMAIN 3 · TASKS 3.1, 3.3

CloudWatch metrics, logs & alarms

  • Metrics summarize behavior over time
  • Logs preserve detailed events
  • Alarms evaluate configured signals
  • Use correlation IDs across job and batch boundaries
Choose / applyExam distinction
Monitor end-to-end lag, completeness and error rates in addition to service health.A CPU alarm alone does not measure data freshness.
Example & explanation
  • Alert when the latest validated business timestamp exceeds the agreed delay.
  • A technically healthy pipeline can still deliver stale or incomplete data. Monitor business outcomes as well as infrastructure symptoms.

CloudWatch Logs Insights & analysis

  • Structured logs support efficient filtering
  • Queries isolate a run, source or error code
  • Retention controls storage cost
  • Avoid logging credentials and sensitive payloads
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use logs to connect symptoms across extraction, transformation and publication.Repeated log lines can be retries of one event rather than distinct business failures.
Example & explanation
  • Group errors by pipeline_id and batch_id to locate the failing stage.
  • Consistent identifiers reduce investigation time. Log volume and retention should serve operational and audit requirements.

Troubleshooting Glue & EMR

  • Separate planning, read, shuffle and write time
  • Inspect memory, spills, skew and failures
  • Check driver and executor evidence
  • Validate connector dependencies and permissions
Choose / applyExam distinction
Fix the measured bottleneck and rerun a controlled comparison.More compute does not repair invalid credentials, a broken schema or a blocked network path.
Example & explanation
  • A long shuffle with a few stragglers suggests skew; an access-denied error points to authorization.
  • Stage-level evidence makes optimization targeted. Repeated capacity increases without diagnosis can simply increase the cost of failure.

Warehouse waits & stream lag

  • Query queueing differs from slow execution
  • Database locks can block progress
  • Stream lag measures consumer delay
  • Destination throttling can propagate upstream
Choose / applyExam distinction
Compare ingress, processing and sink rates when diagnosing a backlog.Raising producer throughput can worsen an already slow sink.
Example & explanation
  • A consumer falls behind because writes are throttled by the destination; reduce write pressure or adjust that destination.
  • Backlogs are system-wide signals. The slowest constrained component determines steady-state throughput.

Alerts, SNS, SQS & failure routing

  • SNS distributes notifications
  • SQS buffers work for consumers
  • A dead-letter path preserves failed items
  • An alert needs an owner and actionable context
Choose / applyExam distinction
Send run IDs, impact and recovery instructions with failure alerts.A dead-letter queue does not automatically redrive itself safely.
Example & explanation
  • After fixing a malformed-data parser, selectively replay quarantined batches with idempotent outputs.
  • Detection is only useful when it leads to controlled remediation. Separate notification fanout from durable work handling.

Backfills, checkpoints & restore drills

  • Backfills reprocess selected historical intervals
  • Version the logic used for the replay
  • Isolate output before publishing
  • Reconcile counts and totals against the intended source window
Choose / applyExam distinction
Test recovery with duplicates, partial outputs and interrupted jobs.A backup that has never been restored is unproven recovery evidence.
Example & explanation
  • Rebuild one daily partition in a temporary location, validate it, then publish a controlled replacement.
  • Backfills are production changes to historical truth. Their scope and validation should be explicit and auditable.

Cost allocation & efficient compute

  • Tag and attribute work to owners
  • Reduce unnecessary scans and data movement
  • Use appropriate execution duration and capacity
  • Consider storage, requests, retries and cross-Region transfer together
Choose / applyExam distinction
Optimize the cost per validated dataset or business outcome.A lower hourly rate is not cheaper if the job takes much longer or fails repeatedly.
Example & explanation
  • Compact files and prune partitions before doubling the query budget.
  • Cost and performance often improve together when waste is removed. Compare complete runs rather than isolated line-item rates.

Runbooks, SLOs & deployment safety

  • Define freshness, completeness and quality objectives
  • Use staged deployment and rollback plans
  • Record dependencies and credential ownership
  • Keep runbooks executable and tested
Choose / applyExam distinction
Practice an incident workflow before a critical reporting deadline.A successful code rollback may not undo already published incorrect data.
Example & explanation
  • Stop publication, isolate the affected batch, repair logic, replay and reconcile before resuming.
  • Operational maturity includes the data state, not just application binaries. Recovery must restore correct downstream records.

Exercise: Investigate freshness with structured logs

  • Find why a technically successful run did not publish a fresh, complete dataset.
Setup
  • Read the embedded log fixture; a CloudWatch Logs group is only needed if you choose to run the Logs Insights query.
Complete worked answer
  • Compare input, accepted and rejected counts for batch b009.
  • Check the published business watermark against the freshness objective.
  • Identify the failed business outcome instead of relying only on status=SUCCEEDED.
  • Define an alert that includes pipeline, batch ID, lag and reconciliation difference.
text
# Structured JSON log fixtures
{"pipeline":"orders","batch":"b009","stage":"extract","input":1000}
{"pipeline":"orders","batch":"b009","stage":"validate","accepted":980,"rejected":15}
{"pipeline":"orders","batch":"b009","stage":"publish","status":"SUCCEEDED","lag_minutes":180}

# CloudWatch Logs Insights query (separate query language, not shell)
fields @timestamp, pipeline, batch, stage, status, lag_minutes
| filter pipeline = "orders" and batch = "b009"
| sort @timestamp asc
| limit 100

Expected result

  • There are five unaccounted-for rows: 1000 − 980 − 15 = 5.
  • Freshness is 180 minutes; it fails an example 30-minute objective despite a successful publication status.
  • Publication should be investigated and gated according to the criticality policy.

Why this works

  • Business completeness and freshness require independent checks.
  • Run success describes execution status, not necessarily the correctness of its input scope and publication decision.

Troubleshooting

  • A count mismatch can also result from mismatched scopes; confirm that every stage is measuring the same logical batch.
  • Log timestamps and business event timestamps answer different questions.

Cleanup

  • No resources are required for the paper exercise. Delete only disposable test log groups if you created them.

D · Preserved source IDs and reasons, bounded replay scope, idempotent writes and reconciliationThose controls limit the repair to the intended records and verify that repetition did not corrupt outputs.

11. Data quality & validation
DOMAIN 3 · TASKS 3.4

Quality dimensions & ownership

  • Completeness checks required data
  • Validity checks allowed values and types
  • Uniqueness checks business keys
  • Consistency checks agreement across sources
  • Timeliness checks usable freshness
Choose / applyExam distinction
Give every dataset an owner and measurable acceptance criteria.A schema-valid dataset can still be wrong, duplicated or late.
Example & explanation
  • A daily ledger needs non-null IDs, valid amounts, unique entries and a timely arrival watermark.
  • Quality rules translate business expectations into automated checks. No single dimension captures all the ways a dataset can fail.

Glue Data Quality & DQDL

  • Glue Data Quality supports managed rule evaluation
  • DQDL expresses supported quality checks
  • Recommendations are a starting point
  • Integrate results into pipeline control flow
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use rules that reflect business acceptance and test their failure behavior.A recommended rule set is not automatically a complete business contract.
Example & explanation
  • Require an order_id to be complete and unique before publishing a table.
  • Automated checks become useful when failed results lead to a defined action. A score without an enforcement or review policy is only an observation.

Profiling & anomaly detection

  • Profiles summarize distributions and missing values
  • Historical baselines identify unexpected shifts
  • Segment metrics by source or tenant
  • Investigate changes before declaring them defects
Choose / applyExam distinction
Profile before choosing thresholds and after significant source changes.An anomaly can be a legitimate business event rather than corrupted data.
Example & explanation
  • A holiday sales spike is investigated alongside duplicate-rate and source-delivery evidence.
  • Statistical surprise and invalid data are different concepts. Business context is necessary to set useful alerts.

Quarantine, repair & reconciliation

  • Separate rejected records from curated output
  • Preserve rejection reasons and source identity
  • Track input, accepted and rejected counts
  • Reprocess repaired records with stable IDs
Choose / applyExam distinction
Quarantine recoverable failures and block critical invalid batches according to policy.Silently dropping failed rows can produce believable but incorrect aggregates.
Example & explanation
  • Input 1000 = accepted 985 + rejected 15; record every rejected row's failure reason.
  • Count reconciliation makes hidden loss visible. Financial or regulatory datasets may also require amount-level and key-level reconciliation.

Sampling & representativeness

  • Random sampling supports broad estimates
  • Stratified sampling protects important subgroups
  • Time windows reveal temporal effects
  • Rare defects may evade small samples
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use full checks for critical key or reconciliation constraints when feasible.A clean sample does not establish that every production record is valid.
Example & explanation
  • Check all payment IDs for uniqueness even if a sample is used to inspect optional descriptive text.
  • Sampling trades processing effort for statistical uncertainty. The acceptable risk depends on the field and business consequence.

Nulls, duplicates & normalization

  • Distinguish null, empty string and missing field
  • Normalize timestamps and units explicitly
  • Define a deterministic duplicate winner
  • Preserve original values for investigation
Choose / applyExam distinction
Repair only according to a documented rule and validate the resulting totals.Replacing every null with zero can alter business meaning.
Example & explanation
  • A missing price is quarantined rather than converted to a free product.
  • Data cleaning is a semantic operation. A technically convenient transformation can create valid-looking but false records.

Skew, distributions & consistency

  • Compare keys and partition sizes
  • Check cross-source reference validity
  • Inspect changes in statistical distributions
  • Keep format checks separate from content checks
Choose / applyExam distinction
Investigate a dominant key or abrupt distribution change before scaling compute.All rows having the same category may indicate a default-value bug rather than true demand.
Example & explanation
  • A failed upstream lookup maps every customer to UNKNOWN, creating both quality defects and a hot partition.
  • Data defects and performance defects can share one cause. Quality monitoring can identify the source of a distributed-processing bottleneck.

Quality gates & versioned rules

  • Version rules with the data contract
  • Classify failures by severity
  • Block, quarantine or warn using an explicit policy
  • Keep evaluation evidence with the published dataset version
Choose / applyExam distinction
Treat quality decisions as part of the deployment and publication process.A rule change can make metrics incomparable across runs if its version is not recorded.
Example & explanation
  • Publish only when mandatory rules pass; retain advisory findings for the dataset owner.
  • A trustworthy pipeline can explain which rules were evaluated, on which data, with what result and what publication decision.

Exercise: Design and explain a quality gate

  • Enforce complete, unique order IDs and nonnegative amounts; explain which records or rules fail.
Setup
  • A Glue Data Quality evaluation or a paper walkthrough.
  • A table with order_id and numeric amount; review the fixture below.
Complete worked answer
  • Evaluate the entire input scope rather than only a sample for these critical constraints.
  • Use completeness and uniqueness as separate requirements.
  • Record the failed rules and dataset version.
  • Block publication for mandatory failures and quarantine according to the repair policy.
text
Rules = [
  IsComplete "order_id",
  IsUnique "order_id",
  ColumnValues "amount" >= 0
]

# Fixture, shown separately from the DQDL ruleset:
# order_id,amount
# A,10.50
# B,7.25
# B,9.00
# ,4.00
# C,-1.00

Expected result

  • Completeness fails because one order_id is missing.
  • Uniqueness fails because B repeats.
  • Nonnegative-amount validation fails because C has −1.00.
  • Use row-level results where supported, or explicit validation logic, to route the intended records.

Why this works

  • The checks address different quality dimensions.
  • A single overall score should not override a mandatory business rule.
  • Recommended rules must be reviewed against the actual contract.

Troubleshooting

  • Do not mix the fixture comment block into a submitted DQDL-only rules file.
  • When a rule is evaluated at dataset level, do not assume its result automatically identifies every rejected row without the appropriate output configuration.

Cleanup

  • Remove disposable evaluation runs and lab-only data according to the test environment policy.

12. Security, identity & encryption
DOMAIN 4 · TASKS 4.1, 4.2, 4.3

IAM roles & temporary credentials

  • A role trust policy controls who can assume it
  • Permissions policies control allowed actions
  • Temporary credentials expire
  • Use separate execution roles for different pipeline components
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use workload roles and least privilege instead of embedding long-lived keys.A role being assumable does not grant it access to the target data.
Example & explanation
  • A Glue job role can read raw objects and write curated objects without accessing unrelated buckets.
  • Identity establishment and resource authorization are different checks. Narrow roles limit the impact of a compromised component.

Policy evaluation & resource scope

  • Explicit denies override applicable allows
  • Resource policies can participate in access decisions
  • SCPs and boundaries constrain permissions
  • Use correct resource ARNs for bucket and object actions
Choose / applyExam distinction
Grant only the actions, prefixes and conditions needed by a component.An SCP or permissions boundary does not grant access by itself.
Example & explanation
  • ListBucket uses a bucket ARN; GetObject uses an object ARN such as bucket/prefix/*.
  • Troubleshooting requires all relevant policy layers. Adding an allow cannot override an explicit deny.

Lake Formation & fine-grained access

  • Lake Formation governs supported catalog data access
  • Permissions can restrict rows and columns
  • LF-Tags support policy grouping
  • Integrated engine behavior and permission mode matter
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use governed table access for supported lake query engines.Granting a catalog permission does not remove every IAM, S3 or KMS prerequisite.
Example & explanation
  • HR analysts see approved employee columns; regional analysts see only their authorized rows.
  • Fine-grained governance works through the integrated authorization path. Test with the actual consumer role and engine rather than an administrator session.

Network access & endpoints

  • Security groups control permitted network traffic
  • Routes and DNS determine reachability
  • VPC endpoints provide supported private service paths
  • Endpoint policies can constrain access
Choose / applyExam distinction
Test connectivity, identity and resource permission independently.A private route is not encryption or automatic data authorization.
Example & explanation
  • A private Glue job needs suitable paths to its database, S3 and any required service APIs.
  • Private placement can reduce exposure but can also remove access to dependencies. A complete network design accounts for each required endpoint.

Secrets Manager & database permissions

  • Managed secrets centralize sensitive connection material
  • Rotation must coordinate with the database
  • Database users and roles control SQL privileges
  • Parameter Store supports configuration and appropriate secret use cases
Choose / applyExam distinction
Retrieve credentials at runtime with a narrow role and avoid logging them.Rotating a stored value without updating or validating the actual database credential can break ingestion.
Example & explanation
  • A pipeline reloads its managed database secret and reconnects using tested rotation behavior.
  • Cloud access and database access are separate authorizations. Credential lifecycle is part of pipeline reliability.

KMS, envelope encryption & S3

  • A data key encrypts data; a KMS key protects key material in envelope patterns
  • Key policies and caller permissions matter
  • S3 encryption and transport encryption serve different layers
  • Cross-account use needs compatible key and data policies
Choose / applyExam distinction
Choose customer-managed keys when key policy and cross-account control are required.Permission to GetObject does not necessarily include permission to decrypt it.
Example & explanation
  • A cross-account reader needs the data access path and the appropriate KMS decrypt authorization.
  • Encryption can protect stored bytes while preventing a legitimate job from operating. Diagnose the object policy and key policy together.

TLS, masking & anonymization

  • TLS protects data in transit
  • Masking reduces exposed field detail
  • Tokenization replaces values with managed surrogates
  • Anonymization must address re-identification risk
Choose / applyExam distinction
Apply the protection that matches the field, audience and use case.Reversible encryption is not equivalent to irreversible anonymization.
Example & explanation
  • Analysts use a tokenized customer identifier while a restricted mapping supports approved operational recovery.
  • Privacy transformations must preserve necessary utility without exposing forbidden information. Security controls apply to temporary files and query results too.

Cross-account & database authorization

  • Cross-account sharing requires agreement across both sides
  • KMS and Lake Formation can add separate requirements
  • Database GRANT controls SQL operations
  • RBAC, ABAC and tags express different policy organization patterns
Choose / applyExam distinction
Test effective access with the actual assumed role and database identity.A successful console login does not prove access to a protected table or encrypted result.
Example & explanation
  • An analytics role discovers an asset but still needs approved table and key permissions to query it.
  • End-to-end authorization spans service APIs, data catalogs, storage, encryption and database privileges.

Exercise: Read a least-privilege S3/KMS policy

  • Explain why a job can list raw-prefix objects, read them and decrypt them, while having no grant to write unrelated objects.
Setup
  • Replace bucket, Region, account and key IDs before using the policy.
  • The intended execution role and key policy must be reviewed together.
Complete worked answer
  • Separate bucket-level listing from object-level reads.
  • Scope listing to raw/ and raw/* prefixes.
  • Scope key use to the one appropriate customer-managed KMS key.
  • Test with the actual execution role; verify trust, guardrails, resource policies and key policy as well.
json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-LAB-BUCKET",
      "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["raw/", "raw/*"]}}
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-LAB-BUCKET/raw/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "kms:Decrypt",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/YOUR-KEY-ID"
    }
  ]
}

Expected result

  • The policy itself grants no PutObject or DeleteObject action.
  • Listing and object reads use different resource ARNs.
  • Successful reading still depends on the complete effective policy path and the actual key configuration.

Why this works

  • Least privilege includes both actions and resource scope.
  • Object access and decryption authorization are separate layers; a narrow identity policy is only one part of evaluation.

Troubleshooting

  • A client listing the bucket root instead of the allowed prefix may be denied by design.
  • An explicit deny or incompatible key policy can still prevent a read even when this identity policy allows it.

Cleanup

  • Detach and delete any disposable test policy only if you created it for the lab.

13. Audit, privacy & data governance
DOMAIN 4 · TASKS 4.4, 4.5

CloudTrail & audit coverage

  • CloudTrail records supported account activity
  • Management and data events have different coverage and configuration
  • Protect audit storage
  • Choose query and retention options for investigation needs
Choose / applyExam distinction
Enable the required event categories before relying on the evidence.A default management-event history is not a complete record of every S3 object read.
Example & explanation
  • An audit needs object-level access evidence, so evaluate the required data-event logging coverage.
  • Auditability depends on what was recorded at the time. Retention and tamper protection are as important as search capability.

Application logs & centralized analysis

  • CloudWatch Logs holds application evidence
  • CloudTrail Lake supports event data store queries
  • Athena can analyze compatible logs in S3
  • OpenSearch supports search-oriented investigation
Choose / applyExam distinction
Select the analysis path according to data volume, query pattern and operational requirements.Application logs and API audit logs answer different questions.
Example & explanation
  • Trace an ETL failure with job logs, then investigate the policy change using CloudTrail.
  • Combining evidence sources establishes both the processing symptom and the control-plane change that may have caused it.

AWS Config & configuration history

  • Config tracks supported resource configurations
  • Rules evaluate configured compliance conditions
  • Historical changes help explain incidents
  • Coverage depends on recording settings and supported resources
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use configuration evidence alongside activity logs.A compliant resource configuration does not prove every dataset record is valid.
Example & explanation
  • Investigate when a bucket policy or other recorded resource configuration changed relative to an access failure.
  • Configuration history describes state over time. Activity logs explain calls, while quality checks evaluate data contents.

Macie, classification & PII

  • Macie helps discover sensitive data in supported S3 content
  • Classify sensitivity and ownership
  • Apply access restrictions and remediation policies
  • Minimize sensitive values in logs and nonproduction datasets
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use discovery findings to prioritize governance controls and investigation.A sensitive-data finding does not automatically mask the source object.
Example & explanation
  • A newly detected identifier column triggers a review of catalog classification and allowed consumer access.
  • Discovery provides evidence, not a complete privacy program. Ownership and remediation processes turn findings into effective controls.

Sovereignty, residency & deletion

  • Track storage, processing, replication and backup locations
  • Restrict disallowed Regions and destinations
  • Retention policies include derived and historical copies
  • Record completion evidence for approved deletions
Choose / applyExam distinction
Design residency controls across the full data path.Keeping the primary bucket in one Region does not constrain every export or replica.
Example & explanation
  • A dataset's replicas, logs, query results and backups are included in its location inventory.
  • Data location is a system property. Pipelines can create indirect copies that violate the intended residency boundary.

SageMaker Unified Studio & projects

  • A unified domain organizes users, assets and projects
  • Domain units organize delegated business structure
  • Projects provide a collaboration boundary
  • Execution permissions still control actual AWS resources
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use the relevant domain type and identity setup for organizational collaboration.Project membership is not a substitute for every underlying data permission.
Example & explanation
  • A finance project works with approved assets under a finance domain unit.
  • Organizational structure and technical enforcement must align. Review project execution roles, identities and actual data access paths.

SageMaker Catalog, lineage & sharing

  • Business metadata makes assets discoverable
  • Owners publish and govern shared assets
  • Subscriptions or approval processes govern access patterns
  • Lineage records upstream and downstream relationships
Choose / applyExam distinction
Use ownership, glossary terms and lineage to support trusted reuse.Discoverability, approval and effective query access are separate stages.
Example & explanation
  • An analyst identifies a revenue dataset, checks lineage, requests access and uses the approved project identity.
  • A catalog helps explain what data means and where it came from. Governance also requires enforcement and a repeatable access lifecycle.

Governance framework & data products

  • Assign owners and stewards
  • Define contracts, quality targets and retention
  • Track purpose, consumers and allowed use
  • Review access and evidence periodically
Choose / applyExam distinction
Treat a reusable dataset as a maintained product with an accountable owner.Publishing files without ownership, lineage or change rules is not complete data governance.
Example & explanation
  • A customer-data product includes its schema, quality evidence, permitted uses, refresh objective and support contact.
  • Governance connects technical controls to responsibility. A framework should make access decisions, change management and incident response repeatable.

Exercise: Build a governance and audit evidence matrix

  • Identify the controls and evidence needed to support governed sharing and residency.
Setup
  • No AWS resources are required.
  • Scenario: sensitive customer data may stay only in an approved Region and be read only by an approved finance project.
Complete worked answer
  • Inventory source, curated, export, backup, replica, query-result and log locations.
  • Assign a data-product owner, classification and allowed uses.
  • Trace catalog approval to actual project identity, Lake Formation/storage access and KMS permissions.
  • Check required CloudTrail event coverage, relevant configuration history and application evidence.
  • Record lineage, quality-rule version and the published dataset version.
text
Control              | Evidence to retain
Ownership / purpose  | Owner, steward, classification, approved uses
Residency            | Resource and copy inventory; allowed destinations
Authorization        | Approved project/role; effective table/storage/key grants
Quality              | Ruleset version; run result; accepted/rejected counts
Lineage              | Source → transformation version → published asset
Audit                | Required CloudTrail coverage; protected retained logs
Deletion / retention | Versions, snapshots, backups and derived-copy policy

Expected result

  • A primary-bucket location alone is insufficient evidence of residency.
  • Catalog discoverability alone is insufficient evidence of read authorization.
  • A job success flag alone is insufficient evidence of quality.

Why this works

  • Governance connects technical enforcement to accountable decisions.
  • Evidence must cover actual copies, identities and data versions rather than a single component in isolation.

Troubleshooting

  • Do not assume unconfigured historical data-event logging can be reconstructed after an incident.
  • Resolve conflicts between deletion requirements and legal retention using the applicable approved policy.

Cleanup

  • No cloud cleanup is required; retain the completed matrix as your study answer.

Incremental processing and recovery

MechanismTracks / controlsImportant limit
Glue bookmarkSupported source processing progressDoes not automatically remove old target output
Stream checkpointConsumer progress or engine stateAn external write can occur before checkpointing
DMS CDC positionSupported source change progressNeeds retained logs and engine-specific configuration
Idempotency keyLogical business action identityMust survive retries and be enforced atomically where needed
Iceberg snapshotCommitted table file setSnapshot expiry removes that historical recovery point
Batch manifestExpected files for a logical batchConsumers still verify completeness and integrity

SQL correctness

PatternWhat to verifyCommon failure
LEFT JOINLocation of right-table filtersWHERE rejects unmatched null rows
COUNT(*)Counts rowsConfused with COUNT(nullable_column)
ROW_NUMBERDeterministic ordering within a keyUnstable choice when timestamps tie
GROUP BYOutput grain and measure definitionAggregating already duplicated joins
AVG of group averagesCorrect weightingSmall groups get excessive weight
MERGEUnique intended source match per target keyAmbiguous repeated updates

Monitoring evidence

QuestionEvidenceLimit
Who called an AWS API?CloudTrail configured activity recordsRequired event coverage must exist
What resource configuration changed?AWS Config history for recorded resourcesNot a record-level data-quality check
Which job stage failed?CloudWatch application logs and run identifiersMissing context makes correlation difficult
Is data fresh enough?Business watermark / end-to-end lagSuccess status alone is insufficient
Are records complete?Reconciliation and quality metricsSchema discovery alone is insufficient
Why is the query slow?Execution plan, queue/lock and scan evidenceMore compute is not always the remedy

Quality dimensions

DimensionCheckExample failure
CompletenessRequired fields and expected arrivalsMissing order ID or absent batch file
ValidityAllowed types, ranges and valuesNegative amount under a nonnegative contract
UniquenessExpected key multiplicityDuplicate current order key
ConsistencyAgreement across related sourcesUnknown customer reference
TimelinessBusiness watermark meets SLOA two-day-old serving dataset
AccuracyAgreement with trusted business realityCorrectly typed but wrong monetary units

Authorization layers

LayerControlsDoes not establish by itself
Role trust policyWho can assume a roleAll data permissions
Identity / resource policyApplicable API authorizationNetwork reachability or SQL privileges
Security group / routePermitted network pathData classification or row access
KMS key authorizationUse of the key for allowed operationsS3 object permission
Lake FormationSupported governed table/column/row accessEvery unrelated storage and engine permission
Database GRANTSQL operations and database objectsAWS account-wide administration
Catalog/project membershipDiscovery and collaboration contextUniversal unrestricted read access

Encryption and privacy

ControlPurposeDistinction
TLSProtect data in transitDoes not hide fields from an authorized endpoint
Encryption at restProtect stored bytesAuthorized decryption can reveal original values
MaskingHide or reduce exposed detailMay retain selected visible information
TokenizationReplace with controlled surrogatesMapping and linkage need protection
AnonymizationReduce identifying linkage irreversibly under the chosen methodMust assess re-identification risk
Retention/deletionLimit how long copies remainVersioned and derived copies need inclusion
